blocks.x: The New Orleans The New Orleans The New Orleans Okay. Grab it? Yeah. Uh, give me a name please. Bill Rennett. Age? 21. Day of birth? 1936. And uh, where were you born? New Orleans, Louisiana. Have you lived in New Orleans all your life? I have. When did you first become aware that there was such a form of music as New Orleans jazz?

First of all, in my estimation, jazz has always filled a lot of places in my life. Ever since I was school enough to understand the music. I was about 12 years old when I was school enough to hear my first jazz recording. It was very breathless.
Mm-hmm. Uh, what did... Your parents and their friends think about it then?

Well, my father, he plays the trombone. He's certainly a fan of jazz. And through him, I became interested in jazz. He's a great team. They're very fond of jazz. Both my mother and my father and their friends. Mm-hmm. In fact, they attend many jazz concerts and get there to New Orleans jazz club as often as possible.
Uh-huh. What's that, you and your friends? My friends.

Well, I... All of them together are very fond of jazz. We... In fact, we hit a band a few years ago that we thought a great deal of. We played for different parties and different yacht club dances and affairs like that. In fact, we made a few recordings. Mm-hmm. It was mostly Dixie Lane jazz that we... Uh-huh. We did our music to. That's modern jazz in any way.

Yeah. Well, that's what I'm talking about. That's the subject between Dixie Lane jazz, of course. Uh-huh. Uh... Have you noticed, uh, using jazz bands at parties? Uh, uh, to, uh, most of the parties you tend to go to hire jazz bands. So, I'm sorry.
You're, uh, you're, uh, not a established friend of how Dixie Lane jazz has progressed. Mm-hmm. Uh, what the reaction to the general opinion of Dixie Lane jazz is, as far as...

Well, what I'm... I'm trying to get the general reaction by finding out when people listen to it, you know, when I heard it, whether they preferred to hire a jazz band for parties or... You don't understand.

Well, the parties that I did attend, in fact, uh... Uh, the parties that I did attend here is my dad addiction man, uh, a jazz band, uh, to supply the music. This band seemed to, uh, be respected. In fact, its type of music was respected a great deal by the people that, at the parties, they seemed to stand to it a great deal and gather around the band and stay to a certain extent.
Uh, and this is, besides the debutante parties, at other dances and such.

Besides the debutante parties, yacht club affairs, uh, in fact, when I was in high school, the, uh, Dixie Lane jazz band was at the senior prom and things like that. Everyone I attended was Dixie Lane. Mm-hmm. It seems to be moving far ahead of the whole-time dance band. Pardon? Hmm? It seems to be moving ahead of the whole-time dance band that used to dominate the parties from...
You mean, uh, white commercial sweet bands? Right. Mostly Negro bands. It, uh, well, um, you mean jazz bands were, uh, taking the, the play away from, uh, from the white, uh, commercial bands, huh?
I, I, I think so. Yeah.
Uh, what about now, at, uh, at parties such as fraternity parties, in fact, do you tend to hire jazz bands or what?
Well, the Sturges and I'm in, we, we, uh, hire, to call it jazz bands. Mm-hmm. White jazz bands are popular, I think. Yeah.
Well, uh, these are, uh, a, a, a jazz bands and not rock and roll bands, huh? Not rock and roll, no. Mostly Dixie Lane jazz bands.
Uh-huh. Hopper Selestine's old bands. Yeah. The most popular people in the set. Uh-huh. Uh.
Well, I think that's... about all these bands. Can you think of anything else you could add on social acceptance of New Orleans jazz?
Nothing offhand, except that nothing can keep going in the future. Okay. Okay. I know they brought you music into New Orleans.
Uh-huh. Well, uh, have you noticed in, in recent years that tenancy for people your age are trying to prefer rhythm and blues to jazz?

Definitely, uh, uh, there's a trend, uh, where, uh, rock and roll has, uh, men, it, it has replaced Dixie Lane to a certain extent. Uh-huh. However, I don't think it has replaced it as much in New Orleans as it, uh, has in other places in the United States. Mm-hmm. New Orleans has always been a jazz city, more or less. And, uh, I don't think that rock and roll will offset the spread of jazz in New Orleans itself or offset it in any way that it will knock it out altogether or anything like that. Uh-huh.
Well, uh, in, uh, people you know, listen to and liking jazz, do they tend to like it mostly as a form of entertainment or dance music or do they tend to think of it as an art form?

I, I, my personal opinion of this would, I seem to think that, uh, they said like it more or less jazz music. It has, it is an art, I'd say, in a sense of the fact that it is appealing if there's any art in.

Well, uh, do your friends and your parents, uh, tend mostly to think of it as just as a form of entertainment or do you know a sizeable number who appreciate it for its artistic content? My parents, I'd say, appreciate it as a form of entertainment.
Uh-huh.
But not as an art?
Uh, I would think so. I, they, they might think it as an art in itself, but it would be more appealing to the form of entertainment.
Uh-huh. Uh, what about your friends?
I think they would agree with my parents and everything.

Uh-huh. Well, uh, I think that's about all. Can you add anything else? Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Okay. Uh-huh. Okay. No, I don't believe I have any more to add on this. Thank you very much. Thank you very much. Thank you very much. Thank you very much. Thank you very much. Thank you very much. Thank you very much. Thank you very much. This was recorded over the telephone on the night of Wednesday, the 14th of May, 1958. The fact that it was recorded over the telephone will account for its poor quality. Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . 1906, that way back.
Have you lived in New Orleans all your life?
Mainly, I've traveled some, but this has been my headquarters all these many years.
When did you first come aware of the pitchfork and hear the jazz?

Well, I had first heard Ragtime, and I was very aware of music and was brought up in an atmosphere of music, taken to the opera very early in life, and we had all sorts of music. Naturally, when Ragtime came in, my father had that too, and I could remember the turkey trots and things like that. And then later on, when I was about 15 and 16 and started going to the fraternity dances, they had the Stella Stance Band, Piron, and all the good Dixieland jazz bands of the city. And gradually, as we grew up, in the debut parties and all the parties that I ever went to in New Orleans, we danced to jazz music.
And debutant parties, too.

Oh, yes, and private parties and other private parties, Tate-en-sons. The New Orleans Country Club had Tate-en-sons on Saturdays and Sundays, where they had the famous Piron himself. And he knew all of our crowd and the ones that were gifted and could dance and sing. And at all the parties, he would act as a sort of massive ceremonies and call on us to get up and do our stuff. We'd sing, harmonize, dance. You really don't see the young people do that as much as we used to, because that was a golden age of jazz. And we danced every night, you know, and in the daytime. We danced, I feel, more than the generations danced today.
What did your parents think of jazz, your parents and their friends?

They were all very interested in it. As I say, my father and mother belonged to a very musical crowd, and they were quite up-to-date. And they embraced that with any other music that happened to come along. They were interested in it and actually had Victrola records for us with that music. And even had, we used to have groups of people to our house and have Piron over there to play for us. My father was always interested in listening to that music. He was a pianist himself. And he thought highly of their technique and was interested greatly in the movement.
Were you thinking of the internet and the phone had an iPhone on music as a sort of entertainment?

Well, he was entertained by it, but my father went into anything in music more deeply than most people would for entertainment. And he really thought it was an era and something that would live. And he was very proud of the fact that it had mostly originated in his part of the world.
How old were you when you were born?
Oh, hey, what, he was about, I imagine, 30-something. I think. When you were born? When I was born.
So I would put him in.
Maybe about 30.
Put him in late 40s, early 70s.
No, not late 40s, did you say?
Late 40s are early 70s when you started going to 40s and having 40s as you have. Oh, yeah. When can you remember his daughter having jazzed into the house or singing into the jazz?

Well, my father didn't necessarily have them. He just was, he knew that we liked this group of Peron and we had a crowd that would meet every Saturday and Sunday. He didn't actually ask them to come to the house, but he was interested. When they were there and if he was home, he was a doctor and was out of great detail. But whenever he was there, he listened very attentively to them and often had conversation with them on their different ideas of jazz because he was such a gifted pianist himself. And my sister was a gifted pianist and she was the best one who ever played jazz up at Newcomb. She had a concert of Gershwin and she was a Gershwin exponent. I guess you could call Gershwin in the realm of jazz.
It's jazz but not New Orleans.
Not New Orleans jazz.
Well, what did your parents think of it? Did they universally like it too? They did.

Some of them were not as musical as my father. But they all condoned it. I mean, I don't have any recollection of any of them thinking it was trash. You know, they all, to my recollection, thought of it highly. Of course, we did too. And I have... Oh, you're friends. Mm-hmm. As I say, we were a very dancing crowd. We sang and danced. And Stella Stan was a hero to me. I mean, I can remember seeing him. I had been away a great deal and I saw him about 12 years ago. And he hadn't seen me because he had been away and it wasn't like the old days when he used to play at so many of the parties where I danced. And he said, well, Miss Esther, he said, I've thought of you often but I haven't seen you around. And I remember you and your sister harmonizing together. He said, and I thought maybe you had made the big time stuff and it's gotten on Broadway. And I said, well, Stella Stan, no, I got married and had children instead. Not that I ever would have made the big time stuff but I said, that statement is a wonderful compliment coming from you to think that I could have. And we shook hands. And I thought very, so I went to his funeral and God was, being a member of the press, we were very near his coffin. And it was a beautiful ceremony, very interesting, highly religious. And of course, the long line of people are all marching with the band. It was very impressive but I think a great, great loss to New Orleans. And one that furthered jazz a great deal.
Well, among the things, back in the 20s, did most of them just think of something to go dance to and have a good time to it?

Well, I'm afraid we, no, Harold Bartell was more interested in our craft than others because he played the piano. And he played by ear like Steve who was Perron's piano player who was so well known. And in fact, Steve gave him lessons because he was interested in Harold. And I imagine, and of course my sister and I who sang a lot, were interested in the harmonizing part of it. But most of them, I would say, were not as devoted in jazz clubs as Menville and Susha and all of them are today. It was so comparatively new that we accepted it as that and didn't realize what history it was making at the time.
What about, you know what you said, they didn't think of it as an art form.
Not to my regulation. I mean, we were all interested in learning it and following. But we had no idea that a real culture was being born right there in front of our eyes.

Well, you said that all the dancers used to go to, did have jazz bands. Do you notice that it's blacking off at any time, having jazz bands, starting to use anything else? Like jazz is supposed to just be a fellow? Just a bit along the 30s or something like that.

I don't remember. It seems to me we always had very good colored bands down here. Most of the dancers that I've ever been to up east. You know, when I went to those big debut parties up on Long Island, they had other, the big name bands, Leo Reisman and all of those bands. But down here, I thought it really stuck pretty much to the colored bands. They had Johnny Detroit at some parties. Was he at the Austin for a long time? Well, you wouldn't call him Dixieland Jazz, exactly.
No, I know he was. He was a white band.
And then the Owls, what were they? That was Dixieland.
I really don't know.
That was Benji White, Ebby Rowe, Guy Lyman, all those guys. Monk Simon.
He met like jazz?
Mm-hmm. Well, uh... They were called the Owls, the group of white brothers.
And you have all your life been going to the same debutante parties. Yes. And you've been all the time at the party.

I never have remembered, even at the patio raw, where most of our... You know a lot of the debutante parties, where we mostly had Pierron and Celestine. There might have been a time there where they had a few white bands, but if so, I wasn't conscious of it. And, you know, I mean, they weren't very good in my opinion, and I don't even remember them.

But what about, uh... you know, the friends interested in it, uh... Are there people who do you know it's among white New Orleans and interestingly maintained throughout the years, during the thirties and the parties?
Uh... whether they wanted it to remain? Mm-hmm.
Uh, well, uh, I'd like to listen to it and prefer to listen to that because it's somewhat of small music.

I think they did. I think that we were... we thought it was here to stay, but we didn't realize, uh, how much of a... of an era, you know, that it was created. You wanted to get that out of it? Yes. Uh, you said you were a member of the press, uh, you were doing the society work, I think it was?
Yes, I had been, uh, several years before I was married, then I was married.
I resigned, and then they, um, needed someone temporarily, and I went back, and of course, on the newspapers, very hard to get away from it, and I stayed and stayed.
How long have you been doing this?

Well, thirty years off and on, but I wouldn't... a great many of those years I haven't been on. More recently, I was on five years, so it has given me the opportunity through these years to have kept up pretty much with activities, even though it was past the age of when I would have been going to debutante parties.
So you have been going to debutante parties every year?

Except during the war, I'd say when I was away most of the time, and sometimes I went from the newspaper to cover it for pictures and things, and then sometimes friends of mine, their daughters would make their debut, and I would go, and it seems to me the most popular form of music all through these years has been Amdic's, you know, and colored bands. Wouldn't you say?
I don't know about three years, but you would say that three years inter-satiously maintained in it.
I would definitely say that. Speaking for myself and speaking for all of my contemporaries, and my daughters' contemporaries, and through the ages, all the groups I've ever had to deal with.
You would say your daughters' contemporaries like it too?
Oh, very much so.
And how old is your daughter? She's 20 years old.
Uh...
Listen, you've mentioned over the years of popular form of entertainment, something to dance to, right? Have you noticed any interest, any increase in interest in the art form?

Oh, yes, I think so. I mean, all over America and in England too. Oh, I'm talking about in New Orleans. In New Orleans, I think the jazz club here is a very enthusiastic group. Harris Duchamp, Edmond, Myra Mendel, and all that crowd. I've never been too active with them because I've been away of Greybill since it was organized and was working on the paper. But I often covered their meetings to take pictures of them. And I thought their interest was very high and has increased all these years.
Would you say that represented a majority of New Orleans people that were interested in jazz?
I certainly would. And a different, you know, it covers all strata, young and old and from different walks of life all over New Orleans. I think it covers a larger suburb of people in New Orleans.
Well, then, you would say that over the... in summer, you would say that over the years, as far as you know, people have liked it? I certainly do.

Most New Orleans have liked it? Have liked it. And I think gradually it is becoming in their eyes a form of art. And I think the jazz club has certainly increased that feeling among the people here. Well, uh...
They've had a chance to study it. Well, you think that... that start in the interest of... of interest in it as an art started, that be after the Second World War?

Yeah, well, uh... I don't think it originated until then. And it has, uh... And it has, uh... Widened its, um... Membership each year. And has, um... Say... Increased the, uh... The people in New Orleans to feel that it is art even now, uh... More than entertainment, which we had always thought. Because as I reiterate, they had a chance to study it in its various... various forms, which the average layman doesn't do. We just listen. But they have, uh... put a great deal... I mean, I'm sure that Dr. Sushaw has. Oh, yeah. I mean, he's been to a great many meetings all over the United States. And I imagine their meetings have whetted the appetite of a great many people to study it further in their clubs.
Well, uh... over the years, you... you say you can't remember, uh... Any... Sousable amount of people thinking of it as trash or gardeners as well. Most people... Most people...
Uh... and I have always gone with a great many musical people on during my life. And I have never, to my knowledge, heard of anyone that thought about it as trash.
Do you think you'd have anything else to add on the line of social status with New Orleans Jazz? What do you have ideas about social status with New Orleans Jazz?

I really don't. But, uh... I'm a joy of being with you. And... I wish that I had belonged to the Jazz Club all these years because I would have been... Um... Had more at my fingertips to answer and to add to your... Little interview. And in fact, it's... I think I will join... Try to join up with the club now that I have more free time.
Thank you very much. All right.
Your name please? Charles L. Dufour. And... Uh... Date of birth?

I was born in New Orleans January the 17th, 1903. And have you worked here all your life? I've lived here all my life. This is being recorded on... Uh... It's leaving Monday 12th of May, 1978. Uh... When did you first become a worker such as foreign music as New Orleans Jazz? I was born in New Orleans. I was born in New Orleans January the 17th, 1903. And have you worked here all your life? I've lived here all my life. This is being recorded on... Uh... It's leaving Monday 12th of May, 1978. Uh... When did you first become a worker such as foreign music as New Orleans Jazz? Oh, I was supposed during my college days at Tulane. I entered Tulane in 1921. Prior to that, uh... Uh... We had... As a kid growing up, we had the relic most known as Ragtime. We had Ragtime records on the phonograph, along with Caruso's and other Red Seals. But the transition of Ragtime into Jazz took place, I believe, back during my college days, back in the 1921-22 period. Now, you realize you're talking to a non-export on jazz, and I'm only giving you a recollection which may not be authentic. Yeah, sir. Well, uh... You said when you were going to high school, when you were going to... When you were going to dance, you were like... Well, I wasn't much of a party boy during my high school days. Uh... I would say what was played in those days was the... Mainly was, uh... What we called... Still called Ragtime. It was, uh... Uh... I can remember the Tuxedo Band was a famous band. And, uh... Uh... They played... They played what was genuinely called Ragtime all the way down until I was... I think about the 20th. That's when the same jazz came into the picture. And, uh... Uh... Just how jazz differs from Ragtime, it's... As a non-export, certainly I'm not in a position to tell you. You get that from Tuchon and Myra Menville and that group. But, uh... Uh... Uh... I would say that in the evolution of this playing... Uh... Uh... Mm-hm... Mm-hm... Mm-hm... Mm-hm... Mm-hm... Mm-hm... Mm-hm... Mm-hm... Mm-hm... Mm-hm... Mm-hm... Mm-hm... Mm-hm... Mm-hm... Mm-hm... Mm-hm... Mm-hm... Mm-hm... Mm-hm... Mm-hm... Mm-hm... Mm-hm... Mm-hm... Mm-hm... But I've never been opposed to it as one is opposed to Mr. E. Pressley. Well, what did people think of it? What did you say, you know, parents contemporaries thought of it? Well, you see, my parents were quite old when I was born, and my father died in 1915 when I was just 10, and it had hardly emerged as an art form. Then it was just, they grew up in the opera house, and anything that wasn't operatic music was clap-craft. The same could be true of my mother, who lived considerably longer. Did you know anything about your parents' friends? What they... Well, I was hardly, at 10 years old, known any of the habits of my father's friends, and, of course, your own great-grandmother was a good friend of my mother's, Mrs. Waterman, lived right behind us and reached back. I remember going to the old French opera with Mrs. Waterman, my mother, as a little boy. So that's how I can say that I know my mother and Mrs. Waterman didn't go on any jazz parties, no man. So that may answer your question. Yes, sir. Well, uh, when you were in high school and college, you kind of had a ragtime or jazz dance at most of the parties you went into? They had, they had, they had those, what they called strip dances in those days, and the, the, uh, a couple of people would get up a comedian and get up the dances, and everybody paid to get in. The couples would pay, and what they paid, paid for the subscription act. I mean, what they paid, paid for the band. There were a lot of, there were a lot of... Now, this is when you were in college? Well, that was, in college, up to my day. I think from my day it began to die out. You know, I, I heard of, talk about my predecessors. But a lot of the guys, uh, a lot of the bands about that time were, uh, like the 6th and 7th band, made up of college boys, or high school boys, who made, I remember, uh, one very fine band was Dick Mackie. You're probably afraid about Dick Mackie around here. In fact, I think Dick lived on the, his family lived on the Gulf Coast, where you are. And, uh, Dick Mackie had a band. And a lot of these boys had bands, and they're grouped into little bands, and they go out and play at their various functions, uh, and make money and break their way through college. And then, of course, they have a lot of the Negro bands, like the Tuxedo, and later on Papa Celestans, and there were others that, I, I, frankly, I don't know much about. But, uh, they were, uh, before you, uh, the parties, before you went to college, the parties generally tended to have jazz bands, or ragtime bands. Well, I had the ragtime bands, yeah. Uh, what about when you were in college, what kind of bands did you have? Well, like I say, I'm not, I wasn't a great party hound, so I'm not in a position to give you any expert information. Uh, but, uh, when they had the fraternity dances at fraternity houses, they'd hire a band, they would play the popular music of the day. And the popular music of the day, uh, well, when, back in the days of Charleston, they played, they played, uh, a piece called Charleston, da-da-da-da-da, I don't know if anything goes. And, uh, uh, the, uh, Black Bottom and all those kind of things that, well, the music went with the, with the song, uh, I mean the dance. The dance took its name, and the music, they were, they were collateral relatives. But, uh, actually, uh, uh, my recollection is that the, well, I think it's been just an evolutionary process. It went from, from ragtime into, into, into jazz. Just what the difference is, the, the jazz musicologists like Sue and Edmond Suchaw and, uh, Myra Menville and, uh, Goop Kennedy knows quite a bit about it. You've talked to him. No, sir, I haven't. But, uh, you would say then that the bands that were playing with U.A. College weren't known about any jazz bands. I couldn't, I couldn't say that with authority. I couldn't, I, I could say that they played jazz, but they, they were not going to fight jazz bands, would call for...
